Rung in fond memory of Fran Brealey, on the bells she loved. Fran exited the Church through the ground floor belfry and out the great west doors to her final resting place in the Churchyard within the shadow of the tower.
Rung half muffled immediately after the burial had taken place out in the Churchyard as the family departed.

Fran and her husband Reg are responsible for the current ring of eight being hung at Welbourn. They financed the removal of the unringable eight at Hagworthingham Lincs when the tower there collapsed and paid for their restoration and rehanging here at Welbourn in 1978.

Fran was a good friend to ringers and you were always guaranteed of a warm welcome when ever you came to ring at Welbourn. The bells were always available if nothing was taking place in Church and Fran would always try to make the effort to be present in person to greet visiting ringers.
Her memory will live on each time her beloved bells peal out.
Rest in peace dear friend.
Rung in fond memory of Fran Brealey, on the bells she loved, who sadly passed away unexpectedly on 20th December 2021.

This quarter was rung half muffled at the request of the family immediately prior to the private family funeral held for Fran here in her beloved Church. All the ringers have connections to ringing at Welbourn and knew Fran. The bells were diminished up to the start of the service.

Fran and her husband Reg are responsible for the current ring of eight being hung at Welbourn. They financed the removal of the unringable eight at Hagworthingham Lincs when the tower there collapsed and paid for their restoration and rehanging here at Welbourn in 1978.

Fran was a good friend to ringers and you were always guaranteed of a warm welcome when ever you came to ring at Welbourn. The bells were always available if nothing was taking place in Church and Fran would always try to make the effort to be present in person to greet visiting ringers.

Fran was highly respected by all in the local community and was also a long standing Churchwarden here at Welbourn. She will be greatly missed by all who had the privilege of knowing her, but her memory will live on each time her beloved bells peal out over the village.

The band wish to associate the following ringers with this quarter and we are sure there are many others too – Sue Waterfall, Gill Gladman, Betty Stracey, Sandra & John Underwood, Margaret Parker, Judy Williamson, Les Townsend, Philip & Fiona Dawson.
The following seems fitting for Fran, taken from Tennyson’s poem ‘In Memoriam, Ring Out Wild Bells’
Ring in the valiant man and free,
The larger heart, the kindlier hand;
Ring out the darkness of the land,
Ring in the Christ that is to be.

(It it is thought that the Hagworthingham bells - now at Welbourn, are the actual Wild Bells which inspired Tennyson to write the poem when he lived within earshot of them at Somersby as a young boy).

Rung to commemorate 80 years since the bombing of Darwin which took place on the 19th February 1942.

World War II forced itself onto Australia’s mainland for the first time, when Japanese aircraft mounted a deadly air raid on Darwin, dropping more bombs than were used in the attack on Pearl Harbour. The loss of life and devastation was profound. This attack marked the first of at least 64 air raids on Northern Australia and attacks continued until 12 November 1943.

On this day as on Anzac Day and Remembrance Day, we reflect on our past, pay tribute to the service men and women who courageously defended our country, and remember all those who were affected by the war fought over Northern Australia.
It was also devastating for the local Aboriginal community, their land had already been taken from them, and with the bombs it was being destroyed.

The Day also embraces reconciliation as Indigenous and non-Indigenous people fought side-by-side to protect our country and Aboriginal people are now being recognised for their contribution to the War effort.

Darwin is also a place of reconciliation with the Japanese people who have now become one of our most trusted and loyal friends in which to create a world of human dignity, human rights, and the rights of nations to live free of coercion and bullying.
Lest we forget.

The Civic Bells pealed out over the City during the Freedom Parade of the Second Battalion of the Royal Anglian Regiment known as The Poachers, as they exercised their right to parade/march through the City of Lincoln with Colours flying, bayonets fixed, bands playing and bells pealing. 350 soldiers from the Regiment took part in this Freedom Parade to mark the granting of the Freedom of the City of Lincoln to the Royal Anglian Regiment in 1997. This is also their homecoming parade after being deployed on active service for the past 12 months.
The parade was preceded by the Civic Procession from the Guildhall down the High Street to Cornhill to wait for the parade to arrive.

The Regiment marched down the High Street from St Martin’s Square, passing the Guildhall and the City War Memorial to the Cornhill a few hundred yards away from the Civic Church of St Mary le Wigford where the parade halted and formed up in Cornhill Square so that the parade could be inspected by the Right Worshipful the Mayor of Lincoln, Councillor Jackie Kirk and Her Majesty’s Lord-Lieutenant for the County of Lincolnshire, Mr Toby Dennis. Also present were the City Sheriff, members of the City of Lincoln Civic Party, the Freemen of the City and other City Dignitaries including the MP for Lincoln. The official salute to the Right Worshipful the Mayor of Lincoln and the Lord-Lieutenant of Lincolnshire was given before the Parade marched off to finish in City Square.

Rung on the back three (the original three) on Michaelmas Day to mark the end of the ringing of the Culfrey Bell (the tenor) each evening at 7pm between Michaelmas Day & Lady Day, a local tradition dating back to the seventeenth century to help guide lost travellers off the heath to the safety of the village.
This quarter was rung up to 7pm, after which the Culfrey Bell (the tenor) was rung for 10 mins.

The Culfrey Trust still provide new bell ropes for the Culfrey Bell, upkeep the Church clock which took over the ringing of the bell, and provide two bungalows for elder parishioners called the Culfrey Bungalows on the site of the old Culfrey Cottages.

Specially arranged and rung half muffled in fond memory of Fran Brealey, on the bells she loved, who passed away 20th December 2021. Fran was a long standing Churchwarden here at Welbourn.

Fran and her husband Reg are responsible for the current ring of eight being hung at Welbourn. They financed the removal of the unringable eight at Hagworthingham Lincs when the tower there collapsed and paid for their restoration and rehanging here at Welbourn in 1978.

Fran was a good friend to ringers and you were always guaranteed of a warm welcome when ever you came to ring at Welbourn. The bells were always available if nothing was taking place in Church and Fran would always try to make the effort to be present in person to greet visiting ringers.

Rung by his friends immediately after the funeral and burial of Robert Wilson.
Robert was not just a friend to many but also a ringer & conductor, farmer & engineer but his passion was inter-war Caterpillar machinery - a true enthusiast.
Over the years Robert has built many frames and done work on bells free of charge at many towers in the Newark area, including building a new frame for Ossington bells and rehanging them.

He was always willing to help anyone whether that was giving his time freely to teach new ringers, help ringers progress or maintaining or improving bell installations big or small. He will certainly be missed greatly by all who had the privilege of knowing him. But what will be missed the most is his big smile, his kind heart and his infectious and distinctive laughter. Robert had a great sense of humour and always livened up a room when he entered!
Above all he was a great friend and will be sorely missed!

Rung in memory of our dear friend Robert Wilson, of Ossington Notts, who unexpectedly died last week.

Robert was not just a friend to many but also a ringer & conductor, farmer & engineer but his passion was inter-war Caterpillar machinery - a true enthusiast. Robert made a huge contribution to the bells project here at Hawton giving his time and expertise freely by fabricating and building the new steel ten bell H frame which involved over 7 tonnes of steelwork, as well as loaning numerous specialist equipment, all free of charge. Over the years Robert has built many frames and done work on bells free of charge at many towers in the Newark area.

He was always willing to help anyone whether that was giving his time freely to teach new ringers, help ringers progress or maintaining or improving bell installations big or small. He will certainly be missed greatly by all who had the privilege of knowing him. We have not only lost a dedicated bell ringer but also a truly genuine person and a good friend to many. But what will be missed the most is his big smile, his kind heart and his infectious and distinctive laughter. Robert had a great sense of humour and always livened up a room when he entered! We are sure he is up there entertaining everyone!
Rest in Peace dear friend, taken far too early.

Achievements: An ivory tablet records the "Year of smiting of Ta-Sety" - where Aha led an expedition against the Nubians.

A striking innovation of Aha's tomb is that members of the royal household were buried with the Pharaoh. A total of 36 bodies which represent the earliest known retainer sacrifices in Egypt. This policy did however prove unpopular amongst members of the royal household as it made it somewhat challenging for those who were hoping for a long career working in the royal household.

On 29th April 1982 V-force Vulcan Bombers - XM598, XM607 and XM597 took off from RAF Waddington overloaded with fuel, bombs and an extra crew member. Flying in radio silence they met up with their five Victor in air refueling tankers. Having refueled  XM598 and XM607 continued to Ascension Island landing after a nine hour flight.The following night XM607 with its attending Victor tankers successfully completed the BLACK BUCK 1 raid on Port Stanley Airfield on the Falklands - dropping 21 - 1000lb bombs on the airfield. Arriving back at Ascencion Island after a flight of over 6600 nautical miles and over 14 hours flying  time - this was the longest bombing mission in history. XM607 took part in 3 of the 5 completed BLACK BUCK raids, and now in retirement proudly stands as gate guardian at RAF Waddington

The Civic Bells pealed out over the City during the Freedom Parade of RAF Waddington & RAF Scampton, as they exercised their right to parade/march through the City of Lincoln with Colours flying, bayonets fixed, bands playing and bells pealing. Marking both bases close connections to the City, with RAF Waddington stand immediately to the south of the City and RAF Scampton standing immediately to the north of the City.

100 personnel from RAF Waddington & RAF Scampton took part in this Freedom Parade to mark the granting of the Freedom of the City of Lincoln to RAF Waddington (25th Apr 1959) and RAF Scampton (14th May 1993).

The parade was led by the RAF Waddington Pipes and Drums and preceded by the Civic Procession which took place from the Guildhall down the High Street to the City War Memorial to wait for the parade to arrive.

The Regiment marched down the High Street from St Martin’s Square, passing the Guildhall to the City War Memorial, a few hundred yards away from the Civic Church of St Mary le Wigford and within earshot of the bells, where the parade came to a halt and a flypast took place.

The parade was inspected by the Right Worshipful the Mayor of Lincoln, Councillor Jackie Kirk and Her Majesty’s Lord-Lieutenant for the County of Lincolnshire, Mr Toby Dennis. Also present were the City Sheriff, members of the City of Lincoln Civic Party, the Freemen of the City and other City Dignitaries including the MP for Lincoln. The official salute to the Right Worshipful the Mayor of Lincoln and the Lord-Lieutenant of Lincolnshire was given before the Parade marched off to finish in City Square.
This is RAF Scampton’s final Freedom Parade with the base due to close in 2022.

The ringing this morning is dedicated to the memory of Ron Applewhite, former member of the local band here, today being the second anniversary of his passing aged 100.

Ron was ringing regularly on Sunday's here well into his 90's but his final ring was here one Sunday aged 96 when he rang the third bell one last time for service. He reluctantly, with a heavy heart, decided to stop ringing then due to arthritis in his hands as he did not want to miss his sally and make a mess of the ringing. However we would still pick him up and bring him to Church so he could listen to the ringing each Sunday morning.

Ron was a member of the Branston Multi Minor Peal band which was highly regarded in the county as the best Minor band during the 1950’s & 60’s. They were known for their striking in particular as well as the complexity of the Minor methods and numbers they rang.
Ron rang his first peal here at Branston and also his last.

Ron died two years a go today aged 100 (4 months after celebrating his 100th birthday which a number of the local band attended and celebrated with him and his family). Ron lived all his married life in Potterhanworth and was a loyal member of the band here and at neighbouring Branston, supporting the bell project here at Potterhanworth which saw the bells augmented from three to six and rehung 2000-2004.

During this evenings ringing we were pleased to see Audrey his daughter, who came to listen to the ringing in memory of her dad and half way through we took a break and went out to the ashes plot and placed a fuchsia on Ron's grave in memory of him. We specifically chose a fuchsia as Ron was very fond of fuchsia's growing many different varieties himself - they were a favorite of his!

Specially arranged and rung with the bells half muffled in fond memory of our dear friend Ron Applewhite, who passed away four months after his 100th birthday on 22nd May 2020.

This is the first opportunity we have had to ring a peal in memory of him and to celebrate his life due to covid preventing us at the time of hos death, last year’s peal which would have been on the first anniversary was cancelled on the morning of the attempt as the conductor was rushed into hospital so we have had to wait until now.
Ron’s obituary:

Ron was born in neighbouring Washingborough but he lived in Potterhanworth most of his married life moving to the village after the second world war and lived here with his dear wife Molly ever since until he had to give up driving at the age of 94 and moved to a sheltered complex in neighbouring Branston where he lived independently for the next for years before finally moving into a care home at neighbouring  Heighington for the last couple of years of his life. So he has lived in this group of villages nearly all his life – all within a couple of miles of each other, so this was very much home.
Both he and his wife Molly were stalwarts of this village sitting on many of the village organising committees.

Ron learnt to ring aged 12 at Washingborough. After he moved to Potterhanworth after the second world war he joined the Nocton band and then got invited to join the locally renowned Branston band. He rang with the Branston band for the next 20 years during the 1950’s & 1960’s. he was a member of the Branston Multi Minor Peal band which was highly regarded in the county as the best Minor band during the 50’s & 60’s. They were known for the striking in particular as well as the complexity of the Minor methods and numbers they rang.

Ron was also actively involved in the Potterhanworth Millennium project to restore the three bells and augment them to six. Not only did he help and support at all the fundraising events from 2000 to 2004 he also helped with the actual bell work. He was over joyed on dedication day (4th Sept 2004) when a life long dream of his had come to fruition – Potterhanworth now had a ring of six bells!

Shortly after the dedication his dearly beloved wife Molly passed away (Oct 2004) after being married for over 50 years and so Ron donated a set of muffles to the Church in memory of her. These are the very muffles that we used today for the peal.

Ron rang quarter peals here on his 90th, 91st & 92nd birthday's and he was very proud of these especially the one on his 90th birthday when he rang inside to Single Oxford Minor and the one on his 92nd birthday which was his last quarter when he rang Plain Bob Minor inside.
Ron was made an Honorary Life Member of the Guild in 2004 for services to ringing within the Diocese, something he was extremely proud of.

We were pleased to be able to celebrate with Ron at his care home on his 100th birthday (26th Jan 2020) as covid had not hit us then so we have some very fond memories of that day and he was so pleased to see us all and to hear about the peals and quarters we had rung for his 100th birthday.
Rest in peace dear friend now reunited with his beloved wife Molly, both of whom are interred in this Church yard within the shadow of this tower (so under the sound of his beloved bells).

Specially arranged and rung in fond member of our dear friend Robert ‘Rob’ Wilson of Ossington. Rob did a huge amount for ringing here at Wellow, not only did he help restore and rehang the bells he also made and constructed the new bell frame. On top of this he continued until his untimely death to week in week out support, help and encourage the local band to keep the bells ringing, in his usual relaxed and friendly manor. His sense of humour, his big smile and his distinctive laugh are greatly missed in the tower by us all.

The band wish to associate ALL the Wellow ringers with this attempt, especially Janet Carr. Also we associate Margaret Martin and the rest of the family, Laura Carr, Margaret Chilton & Paul Sharp (all of whom could not ring today but rang in the first peal on the bells back in 2008 along with Rob). The final ringer of the 2008 peal was today’s tenor ringer who rang the same bell (one of Rob’s best friends).

Rob is a former Ringing Master of the Southwell Diocesan Guild and over the years has given his time freely to help support towers and ringers, whether that be helping with rehangs, making frames or just supporting practices etc. The Guild will be the poorer for not having him around as we all will be.

Final note - Yes we know we have missed off the Nottingham part of the Guild’s ‘new name’ but Rob was against the name change from the outset and so we feel it is fitting to ring today’s peal for Rob under the old Guild Name! We think he would approve! He did only ever ring one peal (his last) under the new name S&NDG the other 131 were rung for the old Guild name SDG.

One of the traditional City Corporation ringing customs as observed since 1728.

Specially arranged and rung at the request of the PCC to celebrate the Diamond Wedding Anniversary of Ray & Rosie Snell, who were married in this Church 60 years ago today!

60 years ago on their wedding day they did not have any bells rung as there were only three unringable and cracked bells here as the present eight bells were still at Hagworhtingham and not installed in this tower until 1978. Hence today's bells are the wedding bells they never had!

Ray & Rosie are long standing residents of Welbourn. Ray is a former Churchwarden and they are both great supporters of this Church, having paid for the complete restoration of the Church Clock a few years ago which had not run for decades. Hence the PCC wished to thank them for all they have done for the Church over the years and thought it would be nice if the bells could be rung on their special day.

Sadly Ray woke up not feeling well with a fever this morning and after a trip to the Doctor’s and some antibiotics was told to go to bed and rest. He was disappointed to miss the ringing but instead listened to it from home with the bed room window open. We hope your feeling better soon Ray, you were missed today!

However Rosie did come down to Church to listen to the end of the quarter and joined the ringers, Churchwarden and some of the PCC members to celebrate afterwards with tea and cake, although not quite the same without Ray being there.

Geoff and Linda Pick came to Staffordshire in the late sixties and over the succeeding fifty years made a huge contribution to ringing in the area, particularly at Cannock. Earlier this year they decided to move to the  North Bristol area to be near their daughter Jenny. Geoff has been an occasional member of the Woodlands Wednesday band since 1997, always willing to ring when needed and happy to help us out at short notice, so we decided that his departure should be marked in an appropriate way. His last appearance as a Staffordshire resident was to be on June 22nd, and we managed to put together an appropriate band, mostly from our regular squad but with a guest appearance from Simon Linford, who was taught to ring at Cannock by Geoff when his father was incumbent there. The band included Steve Askew, one of Geoff’s successors as secretary of the Lichfield and Walsall Archdeaconries Society, and  another successor, Jean Nixon, was originally in the band but had to withdraw because of illness and she wishes to be associated with this quarter peal.

The band’s combined peal total with Geoff was 267, not that high but not trivial. Similarly, Geoff’s total at Woodlands was 24, which made us his third most popular tower after Cannock and Bloxwich. But he is noted not so much for the number he has rung at any one tower, but for the number of towers, 378 in all, and he is the only ringer to have rung peals in all 141 towers in traditionally defined Staffordshire.

We suggested that Geoff should choose the method, and when he told us he would like to ring old-fashioned five-spliced we were slightly concerned that Simon  might be disappointed that there were no new pickled egg methods, but he declared himself happy with the choice.  We had two ringers who had not rung a peal at Woodlands, Simon Linford and Gordon Birks. We did not manage a peal, but Geoff called a quarter of Yorkshire before we went to the pub

Rung to honour and remember William Hale of Painswick; for too long forgotten. William Hale rang here for 42 years from 1880 until he left his home village in 1922. During that time, he was the driving force behind the resurrection of ringing at Painswick after a long period of decline. He taught himself change-ringing and then recruited, taught, organised, inspired, promoted and led the ringing at Painswick; this included restoring the tower's reputation for long-length peal ringing. It was his dogged persistence that eventually led to Painswick bells being re-hung, and he can be considered the saviour of the Rudhall 10 by stubbornly refusing to have these bells re-tuned. Hale was also Hon Secretary for 30 years, setting the standards for all Stroud Branch officers to follow decades into the future.

Ringing on eight today would not have been possible without the enthusiasm of Percy Oram who in 1957 on moving to the county set about teaching a local band - with great success. Encouraging his band to progress resulted in the first QP on the augmented 8 in September 1971 (this by a local band) a second QP in June 1972 by a local band  - jointly produced  the band which rang the first peal on the eight on August 28th 1972 a feat which we celebrate today. The band including two of the peal band, one who rang in the first QP's and Percy Oram's son. The other ringers being associated and instrumental in the developmrnt of ringing at Whitnash. Rung at the Civic Church by the Civic Ringers on Ukrainian Independence Day to show solidarity with all Ukrainians but also praying for Peace & Freedom.

St Mary le Wigford is home to the Lincoln Ukrainian Cultural Center, which has been set up in this Church and the adjoining Church Hall for Ukrainians in the City and surrounding areas, giving them a place to meet and to be Ukrainian together, eat Ukrainian food, enjoy Ukrainian culture and friendship - We regard St Mary's as Ukrainian on Sunday's when they meet! The Church is theirs, its their home, its a little bit of Ukraine and they can do things their way!

To mark the 31st anniversary of Independence in Ukraine (1991), which should have been a day of celebration in Ukraine for them all, instead they are here, displaced from their homes, it was decided to mark the occasion by having a Peace Walk through the City, starting at their home St Mary le Wigford and going up the High Street to the Cathedral. All the City Churches were invited to join in and well over 200 people gathered to take part and support them.
This was a truly wonderful event both happy and sad, and the support shown by the City was overwhelming, and the ringers were only too pleased to contribute in their own small way to the event.

Rung on the back three (the original three) on Michaelmas Day to mark the start of the ringing of the Culfrey Bell (the tenor) each evening at 7pm between Michaelmas Day & Lady Day, a local tradition dating back to the seventeenth century to help guide lost travellers off the heath to the safety of the village.
The bells were rung up to 7pm, after which the Culfrey Bell (the tenor) was rung for 10 mins, and then the bells were rung again afterwards.

The Culfrey Trust still provide new bell ropes for the Culfrey Bell, upkeep the Church clock which took over the ringing of the bell, and provide two bungalows for elder parishioners called the Culfrey Bungalows on the site of the old Culfrey Cottages.

Rung during the anniversary week of the Battle of Arnhem (1944) to honour Sqn Ldr Frank Cleaver, DSO, DFC, who was awarded the Militaire Willems-Orde, the oldest and highest Order of the Kingdom of The Netherlands, for his part in that operation.  As an Acting Sqn Ldr of 570 Squadron, RAF, he flew four missions during the Battle, towing a Horsa glider on the first of these.  On the fourth mission, having completed the supply drop, his Stirling plane was hit.  Very fortunately, he was able to re-cross the Rhine and crash land in a field behind the allied line, and all the crew survived.  The Militaire Willems-Orde was presented by Royal Decree in 1945. The ringers of 3 and 4 are Frank Cleaver's daughters.

On Friday 9th September, Stuart Bracegirdle had the privilege of ringing St. Mary’s bells to mark the death of Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth the Second. For him, this was a significant occasion because on Tuesday 6th February 1952, he had the equal privilege of ringing to mark the death of her father King George VI.

In 1952, Stuart was a ringer at St. Bartholomew’s Church in Rainhill.  Because of the solemnity of the occasion ringing had to be “half muffled” as it was at Weaverham. Therein lay a problem:- they didn’t have any muffles. So, what to do! To solve the dilemma the tower captain cut pieces of carpet and tied these to the clappers and lo and behold, they worked perfectly.

Especially arranged and rung to commemorate the 50th anniversary this day of the first Sunday service of the choir of Hythe Parish Church, Kent, under the current Organist & Choirmaster Dr (now Professor) Berkeley Hill. He grew up in Swindon where his father founded the Swindon Orpheus Choir, and his appointment prior to Hythe was Immanuel Church, Swindon, hence the choice of method. Choice of venue for attempt was predicated thus: St Barnabas was the first church built as a visible embodiment of Tractarianism; the surpliced choir of boys & men in stalls being but one aspect of this; Sir F.A. Gore-Ouseley gave the brass screen-gates here when he was Serving his Title, and the ashes of Sir Basil Harwood (former Organist & Choirmaster here) are interred under the Chancel between the stalls.

To commemorate the recent successful peal here for nearly 120 years, and the above 50th anniversary, the ringer of the 6th presented a clock for the ringing room and set it going, prior to this performance; originally retailed from nearby 235 Brompton Road c1897, to go with the gas-mantle and glass, also restored a few years since (non-working!)

Rung by the local band prior to the morning service with the bells half muffled as a mark of respect and in memory of Anthony Newsum Battle ‘Mr Battle’ of the Old Hall, whose funeral took place at this Church earlier this week (11th Oct).

Mr Battle was Church Warden here at St Andrew’s for well over 30 years, continuing the close link between the Battle family and St Andrew’s - their family Church. Over the centuries many of Mr Battle’s ancestors/family have also been Church Wardens here and so he continued that tradition. He was a staunch churchman and a very good friend to St Andrew’s. He was Church Warden at the time the Village Millennium Project to restore and augment the then three bells to the present six and gave us great support in finally achieving this in September 2004.

Mr Battle is one of the few people who over the decades has served and sat on ALL of the main village organisations, serving on many of them for long periods of time. He has been Trustee, also serving as Chairman, of both the Culfrey Trust and Christ’s Hospital Endowment - the two village charities. Also he has served as a Governor of the local Church of England Primary School and was responsible for saving the school in the 1970’s when closure was proposed. He also sat on the Parish Council and again served as Chairman and as mentioned earlier he has been Church Warden for over 30 years at St Andrew's. The village owes him a great debt of gratitude.

Mr Battle was a true gent whose Christian faith and kindness guided him throughout his life. He never made a fuss but instead quietly got things done with no fanfare and he always had the village’s best interests in mind.
Our thoughts go to Sue his wife, Will & Charlie his sons and their family’s at this difficult time.

In 1434, a local knight, Sir Thomas de Soothill, flew into a rage upon hearing that a servant boy had failed to attend church that week. He grabbed the boy and, lifting him up, threw him into a mill pond, where the boy drowned. Overwhelmed by remorse at the murder, and as an act of penance, de Soothill paid for a new 1300-weight tenor bell for the parish church (now Dewsbury Minster), asking for it to be tolled at his funeral as people prayed for his soul. Sir Thomas also instituted the practice that the bell (named Black Tom after its benefactor) should be to be rung on Christmas Eve, with one toll for each year of the Christian Era, to proclaim the defeat of evil and the forgiveness of all sins, not just his own.

Joan Edna Simpson was born in Louth, Lincolnshire, in 1932.  Her father, Arthur Hoodless was a renown ringer and rang at Barton-on-Humber and St James’ Louth until the age of 91.  Her grandfather, also named Arthur, was the Tower Captain at Barton-on-Humber for many years.  Due to her father’s reserved occupation the family relocated to Nottinghamshire during the Second World War.

When Joan rang her first church bell at the age of 13 in 1945, Winston Churchill was Prime Minister, George VI was on the throne and the Second World War was about to end.  Joan  rang at Cotgrove Church in Nottinghamshire until 1962.  During this time she met Allan her husband, also a ringer.  The family then moved to Southsea Portsmouth where they continued to ring in the Portsmouth and Hilsea area until Joan and Allan returned to Lincolnshire in 1995, moving to Coningsby, where Joan had been a very active member of local bell ringing teams  until her death in November 2022.

Joan continued to ring until she was 87.  This amazing commitment spanning 72 years and her charity work especially for the church and Cancer Research, was recognised when she was awarded the British Empire Medal (BEM) in the 2018 New Years Honors List.  She always said that she hoped the award of the BEM would raise the profile of bell ringing and encourage more people to share her wonderful hobby. She rang her last quarter on 10 October 2018 at Potterhanworth, to celebrate the award of the BEM.
The final words should go to Joan; ‘I have really enjoyed it and it is a great way of making friends’ and of course her mantra ‘listen to your bells!’

Specially arranged and rung at the Civic Church with the bells half muffled as a mark of respect and in memory of Squadron Leader George Leonard “JOHNNY” JOHNSON, MBE, DFM, who sadly passed away on Wednesday 7th December aged 101.

Johnny was the last surviving original member of 617 Squadron, which undertook the famous Dambusters Raid in May 1943, flying out of RAF Scampton just north of the City. He was born here in Lincolnshire being a true Yellowbelly (Yellerbelly) and he regarded Lincolnshire as home, being well known and admired throughout the county.

Johnny has also been a key fundraiser for the International Bomber Command Centre & Memorial which has recently been built on Canwick Hill overlooking the City of Lincoln and its Cathedral (a symbol to the aircrews they had returned home and safe), something which has been very close to his heart - remembering all his friends and colleagues of Bomber Command.

St Mary-le-Wigford Church can be seen from the International Bomber Command Memorial. A quarter peal was also rung on these bells in April 2018 for the official opening of the International Bomber Command Centre & Memorial which Johnny attended.
